issues.legal_issue: Constructive liability for an offence committed by a member of an unlawful assembly depends on proof of a shared common object or the member’s positive knowledge that the offence was likely to be committed in pursuit of that object.
material_facts: The prosecution evidence described a group of more than five armed persons arriving together, dragging the deceased from the temple and attacking him; one person also fired to prevent others from intervening.
The Court accepted the eyewitness evidence and found that the circumstances established the common object and the appellants’ membership of the assembly.
issues.conclusion: Section 149 IPC was rightly applied to the appellants.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 141 and 149 IPC, mere presence in an assembly is insufficient: the accused must understand the assembly’s unlawful nature and share its common object, or have positive knowledge that the offence was likely to be committed in prosecution of that object. A common object need not arise from prior concert, may develop during the incident, and may be inferred from the assembly’s conduct, weapons, and surrounding circumstances; an overt act by each member is not essential. The two branches of Section 149 must be distinguished. The Court relied on Chikkarange Gowda and others v. State of Mysore (AIR 1956 SC 731).

rule.if: group_offence_proceeding and assembly_has_five_or_more_members and accused_understands_unlawful_assembly and shared_common_object and (offence_committed_to_advance_object or positive_knowledge_offence_likely_in_advance_of_object)

predicates.group_offence_proceeding: The case is a criminal proceeding alleging that an accused is liable for an offence committed by a group.
predicates.assembly_has_five_or_more_members: At least five people formed or joined the assembly.
predicates.accused_understands_unlawful_assembly: The accused understood that the assembly was unlawful and was likely to commit an act of the relevant kind.
predicates.shared_common_object: The accused shared the assembly’s purpose, whether from its formation or by joining it later.
predicates.offence_committed_to_advance_object: The offence was committed to accomplish the assembly’s shared purpose.
predicates.positive_knowledge_offence_likely_in_adv: The accused positively knew that the offence was likely to be committed in pursuit of the shared purpose.

issues.definition: When a group-offence proceeding involves an assembly of at least five members, an accused who understands its unlawful nature and shares its object is constructively liable if the offence advances that object or the accused positively knows it is likely to be committed in pursuit of it.

issues.legal_issue: A previously rejected age-based claim cannot be reopened on appeal when the determination was not challenged and the later claim raises a settled factual issue.
material_facts: A claim that one accused was a child had been considered and rejected by the trial court before the trial concluded.
That order was not challenged and had attained finality.
The age issue was not pursued before the courts below in the subsequent appeals, and the Supreme Court was asked to accept a father’s affidavit disputing the school records.
issues.conclusion: The Court refused to reopen the age issue and rejected the claim.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that determination of age becomes necessary when an accused raises the plea and the court entertains doubt. Here, the plea had already been determined by an unchallenged order, and a settled factual issue could not be raised again. The Court also noted that the juvenile legislation relied on was not in existence at the time of the occurrence. No earlier case was cited for this ruling.

predicates.criminal_appeal_raising_age_claim: The proceeding is a criminal appeal in which an accused seeks a determination based on a claim of being a child at the time of the offence.
predicates.age_claim_previously_rejected: A court had already considered and rejected the accused’s age claim.
predicates.prior_age_order_unchallenged: The order rejecting the age claim was not challenged and became final.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal raising an age claim, a claim already rejected by an unchallenged order is not reopened.

issues.legal_issue: A rejected alibi is not established merely because other accused persons’ alibis were accepted; the alibi evidence must create reasonable doubt about the prosecution evidence of presence.
material_facts: The appellant’s alibi was based on a certificate stating that he served as a guard during the period that included the date of the offence.

The courts found no material showing that he was at the school throughout the relevant day, no appointment letter was produced, the certificate’s description of a one-week appointment as regular was implausible, and the attendance-register signatures were not accepted.
The trial court and High Court gave cogent reasons for rejecting this appellant’s alibi, although they accepted the pleas of two other accused persons.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld rejection of the appellant’s alibi; the acceptance of other accused persons’ pleas did not require acceptance of his plea.
issues.legal_principle: Where the accused’s presence is satisfactorily established, the court need not accept an alibi unless the supporting evidence is of such quality as to create reasonable doubt about the prosecution case. Acceptance of another accused’s alibi does not itself establish the alibi of a different accused. No earlier case was cited for this ruling.

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_establishes_accused: The prosecution evidence satisfactorily places the accused at the scene or otherwise establishes the accused’s presence when the offence occurred.
predicates.alibi_evidence_does_not_create_reasonabl: The evidence offered for the alibi is not sufficient to create reasonable doubt about the prosecution evidence of presence.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal challenging a conviction, an alibi is rejected when prosecution evidence establishes the accused’s presence and the alibi evidence does not create reasonable doubt.

issues.legal_issue: An acquittal of some accused persons does not automatically entitle other accused persons to acquittal when direct evidence establishes their presence and participation.
material_facts: Two accused persons were acquitted, while the courts below found direct evidence establishing the presence and participation of the appellants whose convictions were challenged.
The Supreme Court accepted that evidence.
issues.conclusion: The acquittal of two accused persons did not provide a ground to extend the benefit of acquittal to the appellants.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle that the effect of an acquittal depends on the evidence concerning each accused; acquittal of some accused does not displace direct evidence establishing another accused’s presence and participation. No earlier case was cited for this ruling.

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.some_coaccused_acquitted: One or more people tried with the appellant were acquitted.
predicates.direct_evidence_establishes_appellant_pa: Direct evidence establishes the appellant’s presence and participation in the offence.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal challenging a conviction, the acquittal of some co-accused does not entitle the appellant to acquittal when direct evidence establishes the appellant’s participation.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of motive, minor discrepancies, investigative irregularities, or a failure to match each injury to a particular assailant does not undermine otherwise reliable direct evidence.
material_facts: The motive alleged was a stale dispute over a family property partition.
The first information report was lodged soon after the occurrence, and the Court characterized the differences in the accounts as minor rather than material contradictions or omissions.
The injuries were not individually attributed to all the assailants, and the investigation was alleged to have been irregular.
The Court found the eyewitness evidence reliable and accepted the prosecution account.
issues.conclusion: The alleged absence of a strong motive, minor discrepancies, investigative irregularities, and lack of individual attribution of injuries did not warrant disturbing the convictions.
issues.legal_principle: When credible direct evidence establishes the crime, an absent or weak motive may pale into insignificance. Trivial discrepancies that do not affect the substratum of the prosecution case and investigative irregularities do not by themselves require rejection of that evidence. Injuries need not be correlated with each assailant. The Court relied on Leela Ram (dead) through Duli Chand v. State of Haryana and Anr. (AIR 1999 SC 3717) concerning the lack of correlation between injuries and assailants; State of Rajasthan v. Kishore (AIR 1996 SC 3035) and State of Karnataka v. K. Yarappa Reddy (AIR 2000 SC 185) concerning investigative irregularities.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_challenging_conviction and credible_direct_evidence_establishes_offence and (motive_absent_or_weak or discrepancies_trivial or investigation_irregularities or injuries_not_individually_attributed)

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_conviction: The proceeding is a criminal appeal challenging a conviction.
predicates.credible_direct_evidence_establishes_off: The court finds direct evidence of the offence credible and sufficient to establish it.
predicates.motive_absent_or_weak: The prosecution has not established a motive or has established only a weak motive.
predicates.discrepancies_trivial: The differences in the evidence are minor and do not affect the core of the prosecution account.
predicates.investigation_irregularities: The investigation involved irregularities or illegalities that do not displace the credible direct evidence.
predicates.injuries_not_individually_attributed: The evidence does not link each injury to a particular assailant.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal challenging a conviction, credible direct evidence establishing the offence is not undermined by an absent or weak motive, trivial discrepancies, investigative irregularities, or injuries not individually attributed.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court does not ordinarily reappraise concurrent factual findings in a criminal appeal absent perversity, legal or procedural error, or exceptional illegality or irregularity causing a miscarriage of justice.
material_facts: The trial court and High Court both found the appellants guilty after examining the eyewitness evidence.
The Supreme Court found no reason to disbelieve the eyewitnesses and no basis to characterize the concurrent findings as perverse or legally defective.
The evidence included natural witnesses to the occurrence, including a witness unrelated to the deceased, and the courts below had critically examined the testimony.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to reappraise the evidence or interfere with the concurrent findings, and dismissed the appeals.
issues.legal_principle: The Supreme Court is not a regular court of appeal for routine scrutiny of factual findings. It ordinarily will not reappraise evidence supporting concurrent findings unless there is an error of law or procedure, perversity, manifest illegality, or grave or serious irregularity resulting in a miscarriage of justice; it may intervene where a wrong inference of law has been drawn from proved facts. The Court relied on Duli Chand v. Delhi Administration (1975 (4) SCC 469), Ramnik Lal Gokaldas and Ors. v. The State of Gujarat (1976 (1) SCC 6), Mst. Dalbir Kaur and Ors. v. State of Punjab (1976 (4) SCC 158), Ramanbhai Naranbhai Patel and Ors. v. State of Gujarat (2000 (1) SCC 358), and Chandra Bihari Gautam and Ors. v. State of Bihar (JT 2002 (4) SC 62).

rule.if: supreme_court_criminal_appeal_against_conviction and concurrent_factual_findings and findings_not_perverse and no_serious_error_causing_miscarriage

predicates.supreme_court_criminal_appeal_against_co: The proceeding is a criminal appeal before the Supreme Court challenging a conviction.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The trial court and the High Court reached the same factual findings.
predicates.findings_not_perverse: The concurrent findings are not shown to be perverse.
predicates.no_serious_error_causing_miscarriage: No legal or procedural error, manifest illegality, or grave or serious irregularity causing a miscarriage of justice is established.

issues.definition: In a Supreme Court criminal appeal against conviction, concurrent factual findings that are not perverse and are not affected by a serious error causing a miscarriage of justice are left undisturbed.
